articles.title: The LAPD has suspended its use of Flock’s license plate readers, for now.
articles.summary:
Over the weekend, the three-year deal for Flock Safety’s 138 pole-mounted surveillance cameras came to an end, as the LA Times reports the LAPD CIO says it ended the arrangement while working on a new contract that has “very clear terms” about who owns the data collected and what happens to it.
An unnamed spokesperson for Flock told media outlets that unspecified “misconceptions” led to the pause.
[Link: LAPD suspends use of Flock surveillance cameras over privacy issues | https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-11/lapd-suspends-use-of-flock-surveillance-cameras-over-privacy-issues | Los Angeles Times]

articles.title: Professora é afastada após post sobre filhos de eleitores de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Docente do município de Melgaço teve processo de rescisão contratual por justa causa iniciado pela prefeitura após a divulgação das mensagens nas redes sociais.
articles.summary: A prefeitura de Melgaço afastou a professora Marinalva do Carmo Gomes por publicações que incitam violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores do presidente Lula.
articles.body:
Professora compartilha mensagens com incentivo a violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores de Lula no Pará. — Foto: Reprodução / Redes sociais

Uma professora de Melgaço , no Marajó, foi afastada do cargo após publicar mensagens nas redes sociais com conteúdo de violência sexual contra filhos de eleitores do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). O caso foi confirmado ao g1 nesta quinta-feira (29) pela Secretaria Municipal de Educação (Semed) do Município.

As mensagens publicadas pela professora Marinalva do Carmo Gomes podem configurar conduta criminosa, com enquadramentos na legislação penal brasileira, e também violam os direitos de proteção integral garantidos pelo Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA).

Após a repercussão do caso, Marinalva pediu desculpas e lamentou "profundamente o ocorrido". Por meio de nota nas redes, ela disse estar arrependida. "Reconheço que me excedi em minhas palavras e que posso ter magoado e ofendido algumas pessoas", disse - ( veja a nota completa ao final).

Nas publicações, a professora usou palavras de baixo calão e expressões agressivas para incentivar a violência sexual contra crianças por causa do posicionamento político dos pais.

O Sindicato dos Trabalhadores em Educação Pública do Pará (Sintepp), em Melgaço, divulgou uma nota de repúdio às declarações. A entidade classificou as manifestações como inadmissíveis e afirmou que elas não representam os profissionais da educação do município.

Segundo o sindicato da categoria, as mensagens contrariam os direitos das crianças e dos adolescentes, ferem a integridade de crianças, jovens e famílias e violam princípios constitucionais, o ECA e o Código de Ética do Magistério.

O Sintepp também cobrou uma apuração rigorosa e a adoção de medidas legais pelas autoridades competentes, incluindo o Conselho Tutelar, o Ministério Público, a Secretaria Municipal de Educação e os órgãos de segurança.

A docente trabalhava em regime de contrato temporário na Escola Municipal de Ensino Fundamental Gervásio Bandeira. De acordo com a Semed, foi aberto um processo de rescisão do contrato por justa causa.

Em nota, a secretaria disse que "diante da gravidade dos fatos e da legítima indignação da população, a profissional foi afastada de suas atividades laborativas, enquanto são adotados os procedimentos administrativos e legais necessários à análise da rescisão de seu contrato".

"Reafirmamos que manifestações dessa natureza são incompatíveis com os princípios e as responsabilidades que devem orientar a atuação dos profissionais da educação", conclui a nota.

Por que a conduta da professora é crime?

Segundo o advogado criminalista Rodrigo Costa, as mensagens podem "configurar condutas de extrema gravidade perante o ordenamento jurídico brasileiro", como incitação ao crime, apologia de crime, crimes contra a honra e conflito de discriminação de procedência, implicações administrativas e funcionais (previstos no Estatuto do Servidor).

"As supostas declarações transcendem o debate político e a liberdade de opinião, ingressando na esfera da criminalidade comum e da infração funcional grave. Ela pode estar sujeita a responder penalmente perante à Justiça, além de sofrer o banimento do serviço público e do magistério por meio de processo de destituição de cargo", explicou.

O g1 entrou em contato com a Polícia Civil , o Ministério Público do Pará (MPPA) e o Ministério Público Federal (MPF), que informaram não ter sido acionados sobre o caso.

"Eu, Marinalva do Carmo Gomes, professora da Escola Gervásio Bandeira, venho, por meio desta declaração, pedir sinceras desculpas por palavras que falei em um momento de muita emoção e que não deveria ter dito.

Reconheço que me excedi em minhas palavras e que posso ter magoado e ofendido algumas pessoas. Por isso, venho pedir perdão a cada uma delas, especialmente à equipe da Escola Gervásio Bandeira e à Secretaria Municipal de Educação de Melgaço.

Quero expressar meu arrependimento e dizer que lamento profundamente o ocorrido. Peço desculpas a todos que se sentiram ofendidos pelas minhas palavras. Comprometo-me a ter mais cuidado com minhas atitudes e palavras, para que uma situação como essa não volte a acontecer.

Espero que minhas desculpas sejam recebidas com compreensão e respeito. Reafirmo meu pedido de perdão a todos."

articles.title: Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The social networking site is facing criticism for blocking access to the site, which identifies thousands of ICE agents and other employees working for Homeland Security.
articles.body:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.

Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”

In a statement, Bluesky chief operating officer Rose Wang told TechCrunch: “Our Community Guidelines protect people’s safety and privacy by prohibiting the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks. Because the files include the email addresses and phone numbers of individuals, shared without their authorization, we are blocking links to the dataset.”

“When deciding between blocking a link and removing individual posts, we chose to block the links to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary,” said Wang.

In a post on Bluesky, Wang said that the company plans to change the wording on the block message. “We should have changed the wording last night. Changes incoming shortly,” said Wang.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.

“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.

Homeland Security sends takedown notices

Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.

A search site , dubbed Icepick, made by journalist maia arson crimew no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.

Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”

CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.

Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer.

articles.title: LA is just replacing Flock with a different company’s license plate readers.
articles.summary:
In July, the LAPD suspended its use of Flock’s cameras over concerns about how the company was handling its data. Now it’s rolling out hundreds of ALPRs from competitor Axon. articles.title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mistral says its new model can afford organizations a kind of control over its cyber defenses that closed models can't.
articles.body:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month .

The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems.

Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”

The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.

Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.

The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site.

“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”

The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.

Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves.

“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.

Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem.

While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”

Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting.

“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.

articles.title: Utah charges Kalshi and its CEO with illegally promoting online gambling
articles.summary: Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi, accusing it of illegally promoting online gambling.
articles.body: Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its executives, accusing the prediction market of breaking anti-gambling laws, as reported by The Salt Lake Tribune and the Associated Press. The state has filed 14 charges against Kalshi, as well as CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of illegally promoting online gambling. The move marks an escalation in a nationwide battle against prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket. Utah has already sued Kalshi over claims that it’s operating illegally in the state, joining several other states, including New York, Nevada, New Mexico, Washington, Connecticut, and others, in taking legal action against the company. New York and Kentucky have sued Polymarket as well. In March, Arizona became the first state to file criminal charges against Kalshi, but a federal judge later blocked its case. In the backdrop of these legal battles, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is fighting state-level attempts to regulate prediction markets, arguing that it has “exclusive jurisdiction” over the platforms. States recently netted wins with two federal appeals courts ruling against Kalshi and Polymarket’s bid to fight state-level oversight. However, the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in April that the CFTC has the exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets in New Jersey, which recently asked the Supreme Court to take up its case. Kalshi says Utah’s charges are a “crazy overreach” in a statement provided to the Associated Press, adding: “We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona.”

articles.title: Sure enough, the FCC just banned Chinese labs from testing US-bound gadgets.
articles.summary:
“Starting 2 years from now, we will only allow for Test Labs to be based in the U.S or “Reciprocal Economies,” i.e. those places that are willing to recognize U.S.-based testing,” writes FCC chair Brendan Carr. His stated reasoning makes some sense, but it also omits important context: today’s test labs are concentrated in China because that’s where gadgets are made.
[Link: FCC Proceeds on Device Test Lab Onshoring, Reciprocity Rules (pdf) | https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-426300A1.pdf | FCC]
articles.body:
Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech

“Starting 2 years from now, we will only allow for Test Labs to be based in the U.S or “Reciprocal Economies,” i.e. those places that are willing to recognize U.S.-based testing,” writes FCC chair Brendan Carr . articles.title: An AO3 disaster.
articles.summary:
Fanworks hub Archive of Our Own is no stranger to downtime, but an as-yet-unexplained outage of potentially up to a month — announced on the site’s status page — is going to send a lot of fanfic writers scrambling:
> We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks. We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info.
[Link: AO3 Down for Maintenance | https://www.otwstatus.org/incidents/g12jnxck9g6h | OTW Status]
